lesson.title: In der Küche: der Herd, der Ofen, die Seife, der Kamm, die Klingel
lesson.subtitle: the stove and its hearth-cousin, soap's old P→F badge — and a look-alike that is not a twin

hook.title: Cousins, Twins, and One False Twin
hook.content: der Herd and English hearth are cousins, not twins: two old words for the fire-place, *herþuz and *kerþą, that wandered apart at the very start — German hardened the old þ to d (Herd), English kept the th (hearth), the same law that made drei out of three. die Seife and soap are genuine twins from Proto-Germanic *saipō — a word so good that Rome bought it: Latin sapo, the Romans' hair-dye soap, is Germanic in origin, and German shifted the P to F (Seife) while English kept it (soap). der Kamm ↔ comb is the plain twin, *kambaz on both sides of the North Sea. die Klingel is klingen made into a thing — and klingen's own cousin is English clink, the same bell-root with an echo. And then the surprise: der Ofen looks like oven because it IS oven's twin — the same ancient Germanic word, on record since the eighth century on both shores (OHG ovan, OE ofen), originally the cooking pot, with English wearing the v where German wears the f. The stranger in this family is English furnace — Latin furnus, a different root entirely — the look-alike that ended up in English, not German. The kitchen is where honesty pays: cousins, twins, and one beautiful false twin — and the false twin is furnace, not Ofen.

footnotes.title: Rome Bought Its Soap-Word
footnotes.content: Pliny the Elder writes that sapo — a mix of tallow and beech ash — was a Gaulish invention the Romans used on their hair, not their bodies. The word is Germanic *saipō borrowed into Latin, which is why die Seife and soap can be twins across the North Sea while Latin holds a loan-copy.

pattern.title: Hot Things, Closed Doors, Small Machines
pattern.content: 1. The warning frame: Eine Sekunde, bitte, der Herd ist heiß — eine because die Sekunde is feminine, bitte because the stove does not negotiate. 2. Location: Der Kuchen ist im Ofen, die Klingel ist an der Tür — im for what bakes inside, an der for what hangs on the surface. 3. The imperative: Wasch die Hände mit Seife — waschen drops to Wasch in the du-imperative, mit + dative for the tool. 4. Carrying things between rooms: Der Kamm ist in der Tasche — the comb travels, the Wohnen-II Tasche holds it.
pattern.linguist_note: The h/k pair in *herþuz and *kerþą is an old variation inside Germanic, not a one-off: the same wobble separates German Hürde from English hurdle, two words for a woven frame. That is why dictionaries print the hearth and Herd reconstructions as two related forms rather than one word — cousins with a shared fire-place, diverging before either language had a spelling to argue about.

exercises.prompt: In der Küche — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: One second please, the stove is hot
matching_pairs.german: Eine Sekunde, bitte, der Herd ist heiß

matching_pairs.english: The cake is in the oven
The bell is at the door
matching_pairs.german: Die Klingel ist an der Tür

matching_pairs.english: The comb is in the bag
matching_pairs.german: Der Kamm ist in der Tasche

matching_pairs.english: We are cooking in the kitchen

exercises.target_answer: Eine Sekunde, bitte, der Herd ist heiß, Der Kuchen ist im Ofen, Wasch die Hände mit Seife, Die Klingel ist an der Tür, Der Kamm ist in der Tasche, Wir kochen in der Küche
exercises.meaning: a hot stove and one second of patience, a cake in the oven, washed hands, a bell at the door, a comb in the bag, cooking in the kitchen
exercises.explanation: Five rooms' worth of small machines. im Ofen is dative because the cake rests inside; an der Tür because the bell hangs at the surface; and Wasch is the bare du-imperative — the ending left with the hands it washes.

exercises.prompt: Which kitchen word wears the P→F badge that separates English soap from its German twin?
exercises.meaning: Seife ↔ soap: the P→F shift, with Rome holding a loan-copy
exercises.explanation: *saipō kept its P in English soap and shifted it to F in German Seife — the pool/Pfuhl law at work in your bathroom. Rome liked the word enough to borrow it as sapo, so the Latin copy sits between the two Germanic twins.

exercises.prompt: One of these kitchen words is the twin everyone misreads — people call it a Latin borrowing, but it is the family's own, on record since the eighth century. Which?
exercises.meaning: der Ofen and oven are the same old Germanic word — the twin that survived on both shores
exercises.explanation: der Ofen is oven's true twin — the same ancient Germanic word (OHG ovan, OE ofen; it began as the cooking pot), with English wearing the v where German wears the f. The real Latin stranger is English furnace, from furnus — a different root entirely. der Kamm is comb's twin (*kambaz), die Klingel runs on klingen's root with English clink, and die Seife is soap's twin (*saipō).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the warning: 'One second please, the stove is hot'
exercises.target_answer: Eine Sekunde, bitte, der Herd ist heiß
exercises.meaning: One second please, the stove is hot
exercises.explanation: die Sekunde is feminine, so the counted time takes eine — Eine Sekunde, bitte — and der Herd ist heiß delivers the reason. The Herd is the hearth-cousin: German's d where hearth keeps its th.

exercises.idea: you are baking and need the kitchen to yourself: the cake is in the oven and the water is hot
cues: der Ofen — oven's own twin: English wears the v where German wears the f
exercises.target_answer: Der Kuchen ist im Ofen und das Wasser ist heiß
exercises.meaning: The cake is in the oven and the water is hot
exercises.explanation: im Ofen contracts in + dem for the masculine — the cake bakes inside, so dative. das Wasser ist heiß carries the shift story twice over: Wasser and heiß both wear the T→S badge, the kitchen's most common sound law.

diagnosis.slip: the dative in the Ofen phrase collapsed to den
diagnosis.cue: in + the masculine dative is im — in dem Ofen contracts. The accusative den would mean motion INTO the oven, and nobody wants that sentence.

summary.outcome: Run a German kitchen: warn about the hot Herd, bake im Ofen, wash mit Seife, and spot the twin everyone misreads on the shelf.

use_example.german: Eine Sekunde, bitte — der Herd ist heiß und der Kuchen ist im Ofen.
use_example.english: One second please — the stove is hot and the cake is in the oven.

summary.takeaway: Herd and hearth are cousins (þ→d), Seife and soap are twins with Rome holding a loan-copy, Kamm ↔ comb and Klingel ↔ clink ring true — and der Ofen is oven itself: the twin both shores kept, with English furnace as the family's real Latin stranger.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Essen I — der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse — the meal itself, after all this kitchen talk.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from In der Küche: der Herd, der Ofen, die Seife, der Kamm, die Klingel (The cake is in the oven and the water is hot):
twist.target_answer: Der Kuchen ist im Ofen und das Wasser ist heiß
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Kuchen ist im Ofen und das Wasser ist heiß" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of In der Küche: der Herd, der Ofen, die Seife, der Kamm, die Klingel without relying on short-term echo.

herd.context_phrase: Der Topf steht auf dem Herd.
herd.context_translation: The pot is on the stove.
herd.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic herth; English hearth is a direct cognate, the English th corresponding to German d. [wiktionary]

ofen.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist noch im Ofen.
ofen.context_translation: The cake is still in the oven.
ofen.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic ofn; English oven is a direct cognate from the same Germanic word, differing only in the vowel. [wiktionary]

seife.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic saipo, from the PIE root seyb, meaning to pour or trickle; English soap is a direct cognate, its p corresponding to German f after the High German shift. [wiktionary]

kamm.context_phrase: Ich brauche einen Kamm für die Haare.
kamm.context_translation: I need a comb for my hair.
kamm.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kambaz, from PIE gombhos, meaning tooth; English comb is a direct cognate, and both keep the old idea that a comb is full of teeth. [wiktionary]

klingel.context_phrase: Die Klingel läutet an der Tür.
klingel.context_translation: The doorbell is ringing at the door.
klingel.etymology_derivation: From the verb klingen, meaning to ring or sound; the same Germanic kling root underlies English clink. [wiktionary]

sekunde.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin secunda, short for pars minuta secunda, the second small part of the hour — the same Latin phrase behind English second. [wiktionary]

küche.context_translation: We are cooking in the kitchen.

tür.etymology_derivation: d → t with vowel mutation to ü.

bad.etymology_derivation: Final th shifted to d (devoiced in pronunciation to [t]). Verb: baden (to bathe).

kuchen.context_translation: Would you like a piece of cake?
kuchen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōkô; Wiktionary names only Dutch koek — see Apfelkuchen. [wiktionary]

durstig.context_phrase: Nach dem Lauf bin ich durstig.
durstig.context_translation: After the run, I am thirsty.
durstig.etymology_derivation: Equivalent to Durst plus -ig. English thirsty carries the old th where the German base Durst has d. [wiktionary]

feld.context_phrase: Der Bauer arbeitet auf dem Feld.
feld.context_translation: The farmer works in the field.
feld.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *felþuz: the p → f labial shift is the visible law; both languages independently hardened the old þ to d (field, Feld), so no dental shift separates them. [wiktionary]

seitdem.context_phrase: Seitdem ich hier wohne, fahre ich Rad.
seitdem.context_translation: Since I live here, I cycle.
seitdem.etymology_derivation: Seit (since) plus dem (that — the th-to-d twin of the/that); literally since-that, since then, as adverb and conjunction. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
